The problem is governed by Euler-Bernoulli beam theory under small-deformation, linear-elastic assumptions.
The beam has a rectangular cross-section of width b and height h, with the neutral axis passing through the centroid of the cross-section.
The longitudinal axis is x, the vertical axis is y (positive upward from the neutral axis), and the transverse axis is z (out of plane).
The beam is subjected to a combination of transverse bending loading and an applied concentrated moment, producing an internal bending moment M(x) that varies along the length.
Plane sections perpendicular to the axis remain plane and perpendicular after deformation; shear deformation is neglected.
Material is homogeneous, isotropic, and linear-elastic with Young's modulus E.
Deformations are small, so linearized strain-displacement relations apply.
The axial strain at a point (x, y) is ε_xx = -y * d²w/dx², where w(x) is the transverse deflection.
The axial stress at a point (x, y) is σ_xx = E * ε_xx = -E * y * d²w/dx².
The internal bending moment is related to curvature by M(x) = E * I * d²w/dx², where I is the second moment of area of the cross-section about the neutral axis.
For the rectangular cross-section, I = b * h³ / 12.
The bending stress at an arbitrary fiber at distance y from the neutral axis is σ_xx(x, y) = -M(x) * y / I.
The stress distribution is linear in y, zero at the neutral axis (y = 0), and reaches maximum magnitude at the outermost fibers (y = ±h/2).
The maximum tensile and compressive bending stresses are σ_max = M(x) * (h/2) / I = 6 * M(x) / (b * h²).
The internal bending moment M(x) is determined from equilibrium of the applied transverse loads and the concentrated moment together with the support reactions; the specific expression for M(x) depends on the support conditions and load positions.
The relevant response quantities to report are: the bending moment distribution M(x), the bending stress field σ_xx(x, y), the maximum fiber stresses at each critical section, and the corresponding deflection w(x) if required.
No shear stress or axial force contributions are included; the analysis is pure-bending in the sense that transverse shear effects on the normal stress distribution are neglected.
